content.thinking:
I need to lay out the causal chain without exact figures, using placeholders instead. The core symptom was that account pages became slow with p95 latency climbing noticeably during the incident while error rates stayed flat compared to before, which points away from outright failures and toward a performance degradation.

The root appears to be account pages waiting on io-pricing's basket-total calls, which slowed dramatically starting around a point I'll mark as {began}, citing the relevant record rather than a raw timestamp. I trace this further to basket_total having no enforced time limit, so io-shop waited indefinitely on io-pricing — though that's a static-code finding I haven't verified against runtime behavior.

For why io-pricing itself slowed, the evidence is thinner: restarting it resolved the issue, suggesting internal state corruption, but I can rule out production changes, flag changes, or changes to io-shop as triggers. I'm left without a confirmed root cause for the io-pricing slowdown itself, so I need to flag that gap honestly rather than overstate certainty, noting the unlimited-wait finding as unverified where relevant.

This points toward action items: adding a timeout on the optional dependency, investigating the unexplained io-pricing slowdown with the platform team, and adding alerting on dependency latency since detection here relied on a slow p95-based alert rather than catching the wait pattern directly. For recovery, I note the restart as the mitigation step and the metrics returning to normal afterward.

action_items.item: Work with checkout-platform, the owner of io-pricing, to find out why basket-total calls became slow from the onset and what the restart cleared. Record the finding.
Add a latency alert on io-pricing's basket-total calls, so a slow dependency is flagged directly and early, ahead of io-shop's latency alert.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages. The latency series behind the HighLatency alert averaged {series_while_broken} while broken, against {series_before} before, and peaked at {series_at_worst}. Failed requests did not rise ({errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before), so the harm was delay, not errors.

Each account page waited on io-pricing's basket-total call, and that call became slow from {began}. io-shop logged slow upstream calls of {G9feb.1} to pricing. The same minute the slow calls began matches the onset the Investigator placed.

io-shop waited out the whole slow call because, as far as the unverified reading of the source shows, basket_total set no limit on its wait. The basket total is optional, and the account page already renders without it when pricing fails. io-shop did not retry, fall back or give up. It only logged that the call was slow and kept waiting, so the dependency's slowdown became io-shop's latency in full. This step rests only on a static reading that nothing ran.

io-pricing slowed at {began}. The record does not show why. Restarting io-pricing was followed by the service no longer being at the incident's level, and the action was judged confirmed, but no cause inside io-pricing was seen. The record rules out a change on the io-shop side: no production changes were read back for the day before the onset, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: io-shop had no limit on its wait for an optional dependency, so a slow io-pricing slowed every account page. The proposed fix is not yet merged.
The reason io-pricing became slow was not established. The restart cleared the symptom, but the record shows no cause inside io-pricing, so it could recur.

The alert was on io-shop's own latency and fired only after its rule had waited {rule_waits} with the condition holding. No alert on io-pricing's own latency was seen in the record, so the dependency was not flagged directly.

input.executive_summary: For a stretch of {duration}, from {began} to {back_to_normal}, account pages on the shop were noticeably slow for shoppers. Slow responses were the harm. The share of failed requests did not rise: it was {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before. The slow-response measure that paged averaged {series_while_broken} while broken, against {series_before} before, and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The delay came from an internal pricing service that became slow. The shop waited for it on every account page, even though the page can be shown without the price. Argus restarted the pricing service, and the metrics returned to normal. Argus also drafted a code change that makes the shop give up on a slow pricing call and show the page without the basket total. That change is not yet merged. The record does not show why the pricing service slowed.

got_lucky: The slowdown caused no rise in failed requests, so shoppers saw slow pages, not broken ones.
The metrics were back to normal at {back_to_normal}, soon after the restart. The record cannot separate the restart's effect from the slowdown ending on its own.
went_well: Argus read metrics, changes, flags and logs, and named the slow dependency as the leading candidate within about a minute of the page.
The mitigation was reversible: the restart left nothing to put back. Metrics returned to normal and the paging rule stopped firing.
Code-Fix proposed a draft pull request that gives up on a slow pricing call and lets the page render without the basket total.
went_wrong: The onset was {began} and the alert fired at {alert_raised}, so shoppers were affected before anyone was paged. Part of that delay is the rule's {rule_waits} wait.
The record does not show why io-pricing slowed, so the underlying fault is not understood.

input.root_cause: io-shop called io-pricing for the basket total, which the account page can do without, but set no limit on how long it would wait. When io-pricing slowed, every account page waited out the slow call, so a dependency's slowdown became io-shop's latency. This comes from a static reading of the code (F1) that nothing ran, so it is unverified. The record does not show why io-pricing itself slowed.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow to load
